briefs.neonatal-rash:
Rashes in the Newborn and Infant

benign newborn rashes sorted by onset, then the diaper rash split by its folds · reassure, remove a cause, or treat what was addedHow old is the baby, is there a removable cause or a red flag, and does the diaper rash involve the creases?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

Reassure when a benign, self-limited rash has no modifiable cause; remove the trigger when it has an identifiable, removable one. Sort by onset age first. A rash outside its window, erythema toxicum-like pustules on the palms or soles, vesicles or crusting, or a febrile or irritable infant is not benign until the dangerous mimics are excluded. Any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex virus (HSV) until proven otherwise: polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and IV acyclovir.

  • Erythema toxicum neonatorum: firm yellow-white pustules on a blotchy red base, on the face, trunk and proximal limbs; palms and soles usually spared; a well infant. The diagnosis is usually clinical; a smear, rarely needed, shows eosinophils.
  • Transient neonatal pustular melanosis: pustules without surrounding erythema that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; may involve the palms and soles; more common in darker skin; neutrophils.
  • Milia: firm pearly white papules on the nose and cheeks, no erythema; retained keratin.
  • Miliaria rubra: blocked sweat glands; fine red papules and vesicles on occluded, covered and intertriginous skin (neck, axillae, groin). Its cause is in the history (a onesie under pajamas under a fleece swaddle), so treat it by unwrapping the baby, not by waiting it out. Superficial 1- to 2-mm vesicles are miliaria crystallina, usually before 2 weeks; the HSV rule still applies until herpes is excluded.
  • Neonatal cephalic pustulosis: red papules and pustules on the face and scalp only; no comedones, unlike true neonatal acne (closed comedones); linked to Malassezia.
  • Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy yellow scale on the scalp (cradle cap), with redness in the folds; usually not itchy, and the infant looks content.
  • Diaper rash: irritant contact dermatitis, the most common, sits on the convex skin the wet diaper touches and usually spares the creases; Candida involves the creases, with satellite papules. A rash that got better on a barrier and then got worse has acquired something the barrier does not treat.
Diagnosis
Diaper rash: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Candidal diaper dermatitisYeast, on its own or on top of irritation; after diarrhea or antibiotics, or with thrush; the second most common diaper rashBeefy-red plaques in the creases with satellite papules; worse despite the barrier
Irritant contact dermatitisUrine and stool on convex skin; the commonest diaper rashUsually spares the creases; no satellites; responds to a barrier
Perianal group A streptococcal diseaseBacterial; painful defecation and stool withholdingBright red, sharply demarcated perianal rash, with or without anal fissures
ScabiesMite; refractory diaper rash in an infant with itchy contactsDiffuse: trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles
Acrodermatitis enteropathicaZinc deficiency; rare and refractoryChronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis plus alopecia
Sexually transmitted infection, can't missThe concern behind any genital rashVerrucous papules of human papillomavirus, ulcers with fever and adenopathy of HSV, or mucopurulent discharge of gonorrhea and chlamydia
Practice
  1. 2-day-old boy has a blotchy rash noticed this morning Breastfeeding well; born at term after an uncomplicated delivery red macules with central yellow-white pustules on trunk and proximal limbs palms and soles spared Afebrile · HR 136/min · well appearing → Erythema toxicum neonatorum → firm yellow-white pustules on a blotchy red base over the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the palms and soles, in a well 2-day-old: a clinical diagnosis that needs only reassurance. Neonatal herpes brings clustered vesicles on a red base, and staphylococcal pustulosis brings honey-colored crusts in the diaper area or at a wound
  2. 2-week-old boy has had a rash on his neck and chest for 2 days Dressed in a onesie, pajamas and a fleece swaddle tiny red papules on the neck and upper chest; no pustules or vesicles Afebrile · well appearing → Miliaria rubra → small red papules on covered skin under three layers are blocked sweat ducts, so remove the extra layers. Vesicles of any kind in a neonate would first need herpes simplex excluded. Erythema toxicum appears in the first days as pustules on a blotchy red base, and neonatal acne brings closed comedones on the face
  3. 1-day-old boy has spots that were present at birth Born at term; breastfeeding well small pustules without surrounding redness on chin, neck and back some ruptured, leaving brown macules with a collarette of scale Afebrile · well appearing → Transient neonatal pustular melanosis → pustules present at birth, without surrounding erythema, that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; a smear would show neutrophils. Reassure: the pustules clear in days and the pigment fades over weeks to months. Erythema toxicum pustules sit on a red base, and congenital syphilis is a maculopapular rash with no pustules
  4. 2-week-old boy has been irritable and feeding poorly for 1 day a cluster of vesicles on a red base on the scalp Born vaginally at term; no rash before yesterday T 37.9 °C · HR 172/min → Neonatal herpes simplex → clustered vesicles on a red base in an irritable 2-week-old: any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex until proven otherwise, so send PCR and start IV acyclovir. Erythema toxicum appears in the first days in a well baby, and miliaria rubra follows overbundling
  5. 1-day-old girl is examined before discharge Born at term; feeding well; mother asks about bumps on the nose 1-mm firm pearly white papules across the nose and cheeks no surrounding redness; no pustules Afebrile · HR 140/min → Milia → pearly white papules of retained keratin on the nose and cheeks with no erythema, present at birth: reassure; they usually clear within the first month and may persist into the second or third month; do not extract them. Cephalic pustulosis brings red papules and pustules from about the third week, and miliaria rubra red papules on covered skin
  6. 6-week-old boy has had scaling on his scalp for 3 weeks greasy yellow scale over the crown mild redness in the neck creases Not scratching; content and feeding well Afebrile · weight gain normal → Seborrheic dermatitis → greasy yellow scale on the scalp with redness in the folds in a content infant: reassure; it is self-limited, and an emollient with gentle brushing can loosen the scale. Atopic dermatitis is the main differential; this rash is usually not itchy. Tinea capitis brings patchy hair loss ⚠︎
  7. 3-week-old girl has had a rash on her neck and underarms for 2 days Kept in a fleece swaddle over footed pajamas in a warm room fine red papules in the neck folds and axillae Afebrile · feeding well · well appearing → Lighter, cooler clothing → blocked sweat ducts under too many layers in a warm room: the cause is in the history, so remove it with thin cotton, a cool room and no overbundling. Nystatin treats yeast in the diaper creases, and reassurance without changes leaves the cause in place
  8. 10-day-old girl has a cluster of blisters on her scalp vesicles grouped on a red base, 1 cm across Born vaginally at term; feeding well; no other skin lesions Afebrile · HR 150/min · alert → HSV PCR and IV acyclovir → any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex virus until proven otherwise, even in a well, afebrile baby: send HSV PCR and start IV acyclovir. Reassurance misses an infection that can disseminate, and mupirocin treats the honey-crusted pustules of staphylococcal pustulosis
  9. 4-month-old boy has had a diaper rash for 5 days beefy-red plaques involving the inguinal creases satellite papules beyond the border No new soaps or wipes; stools normal Afebrile · well appearing → Topical nystatin → creases involved, with satellite papules, is Candida: a topical antifungal such as nystatin, applied with every diaper change, under the barrier. Zinc oxide alone treats irritant dermatitis, which usually spares the creases, and a steroid does not treat the yeast
  10. 4-month-old girl is seen for a well-child visit flat blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks Present since birth, her parents say; no other skin findings Growing and developing normally Afebrile · HR 128/min → Document the finding and reassure → blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, are benign and self-resolving by age 3 to 5 years; documenting them prevents confusion with non-accidental trauma. A skeletal survey and a report are for injuries, not birthmarks
  11. 3-day-old boy has a rash noted at his newborn check Breastfeeding well; mother had a cold sore last year yellow-white pustules on blotchy red bases, face and trunk palms, soles spared; no vesicles T 37.0 °C · well appearing → Reassurance only → pustules on a red base over the face and trunk, sparing the palms and soles, in a well newborn: reassure; they fade over 5 to 7 days and may recur for several weeks. A maternal cold sore does not make this herpes: neonatal HSV usually brings clustered vesicles; those without them usually have eye, mouth or central nervous system disease, and these are pustules on a red base in a well newborn; base the diagnosis on the morphology and the baby's well appearance. Congenital syphilis is maculopapular, includes the palms and soles and has no pustules
  12. 3-week-old girl has had bumps on her face for 4 days red papules and pustules on cheeks, forehead and scalp no comedones Trunk, palms and soles clear; feeding well Afebrile · well appearing → Neonatal cephalic pustulosis → red papules and pustules confined to the face and scalp, often from the third week, with no comedones, linked to Malassezia: observe; it generally resolves without treatment over weeks to months, and a topical antifungal such as ketoconazole can be used safely and may help. Erythema toxicum peaks in the first days and involves the trunk; miliaria rubra favors covered skin
  13. 6-day-old boy has sores at his circumcision site Circumcised on day 2; feeding well a few pustules and flaccid blisters around the site some ruptured to honey-colored crusts; skin elsewhere normal Afebrile · HR 140/min → Topical mupirocin → localized pustules and flaccid blisters that rupture to honey-colored crusts at a wound are staphylococcal pustulosis: topical mupirocin. Reassurance leaves a bacterial infection untreated, and acyclovir is for clustered vesicles on a red base
  14. 14-month-old girl has had a diaper rash for 10 days It faded on zinc oxide paste, then spread over 3 days Gastroenteritis last week, now resolved beefy-red plaques into the inguinal folds with satellite papules Afebrile · playful → Topical nystatin under the barrier → a rash that improved on barrier therapy and then worsened has acquired something the barrier does not treat; creases and satellites name Candida, seeded after the diarrhea. Add a topical antifungal under the barrier, not instead of it. Topical agents are preferred for superficial infection, so oral fluconazole is not the step
  15. 8-month-old boy has had a red diaper rash for 2 days mild erythematous papules and plaques over the buttocks and thighs inguinal creases spared; no satellite lesions Eating and sleeping normally Afebrile · well appearing → Barrier ointment with more frequent diaper changes → convex skin involved and creases spared, with no satellites, is irritant contact dermatitis, the most common diaper rash: a barrier such as zinc oxide or petrolatum and frequent changes. Nystatin is for yeast in the creases, and a short course of a low-potency steroid is for rashes that do not improve within 2 to 3 days, or moderate to severe cases
  16. 3-year-old girl has had pain with bowel movements for 1 week bright red, sharply demarcated perianal plaque a small anal fissure Withholding stool for 3 days; toilet trained Afebrile · abdomen soft → Oral amoxicillin → a bright red, sharply demarcated perianal rash with a fissure and painful defecation is perianal group A streptococcal disease: oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin. Nystatin treats yeast, and a barrier alone leaves the bacterial infection untreated
  17. 4-month-old boy has had a diaper rash for 3 days Taking amoxicillin for otitis media, day 6 of 10 beefy-red confluent rash in the inguinal creases white plaques on the buccal mucosa Afebrile · feeding well → Topical nystatin to the diaper area plus oral nystatin → creases involved after antibiotics, with oral thrush, is yeast in both places: topical nystatin to the diaper area plus oral nystatin for the mouth. Stopping the amoxicillin leaves the yeast untreated, and hydrocortisone does not treat it
  18. 5-month-old boy has a diaper rash that has not cleared with barrier cream papules also on the trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles His mother itches at night Afebrile · well appearing → Scabies → a refractory diaper rash that also involves the trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles, with an itchy household contact, is scabies: permethrin for the infant and all household contacts. Yeast and irritant dermatitis stay in the diaper area
  19. 7-month-old girl has had a perineal rash for 6 weeks despite treatment red, crusted plaques around the mouth and in the diaper area diffuse hair loss Chronic diarrhea for 2 months Afebrile · irritable → Acrodermatitis enteropathica → chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis plus alopecia, with a refractory perineal rash, is zinc deficiency: oral zinc supplementation. A yeast rash stays in the diaper area without perioral or scalp findings, and atopic dermatitis does not explain the diarrhea or the hair loss
  20. 11-month-old girl has had a diaper rash for 4 days Recovered last week from 5 days of watery diarrhea beefy-red plaques in the inguinal creases satellite papules at the border Afebrile · well appearing → Fecal bacteria raise local pH and compromise the skin barrier → stool raises the local pH (the breakdown of urinary urea), which can increase fecal enzyme activity and further damage the skin; Candida albicans from the gut then colonizes the broken skin. Zinc depletion needs chronic diarrhea with perioral dermatitis and alopecia
  21. 10-month-old girl has had a diaper rash for 1 week beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases satellite lesions beyond the border Her parent asks which treatments are safe Afebrile · well appearing → A high-potency topical corticosteroid → high-potency steroids should not be used on the groin or under occlusion, except in rare situations and for short durations, and a diaper occludes; atrophy and striae are the risk. Nystatin under a barrier is the treatment
  22. 4-year-old girl has had vulvar itching for 3 days Toilet trained; finished amoxicillin for otitis media last week erythema over vulva and perineum into the inguinal creases satellite papules; thick white discharge at the introitus Afebrile → Candidal vulvovaginitis → redness of the vulva and perineum into the creases with satellite papules and a thick white discharge after antibiotics is yeast: a topical antifungal such as nystatin. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases, and perianal streptococcal disease is a sharply demarcated perianal rash
How NBME framed it: question 1

2-day-old girl examined before discharge home Term baby; uncomplicated pregnancy; spontaneous vaginal delivery length 50 cm · weight 3515 g · T 36.8 °C · HR 128/min · respirations 38/min · BP 70/54 mm Hg rash all over: tiny yellow papules on red skin mostly on the trunk

Most appropriate next step?

Competing answers
  • Lesion culture and antibiotics against Staphylococcus aureus: pustules suggest a bacterial infection; but impetigo is a superficial erosion with a honey-colored crust, and localized disease takes topical mupirocin.
  • Herpes simplex virus culture of a lesion: any newborn rash raises herpes; but herpes gives grouped vesicles, and these are papules on a red base in a well baby.
  • Potassium hydroxide prep of a scraping for Candida: papules on a red base could be yeast; but yeast sits in the diaper area as beefy-red plaques with satellite pustules, and this rash is on the trunk.
  • Topical corticosteroid: the skin is inflamed; but a self-limited rash needs no steroid.

Down to two: reassurance or a herpes culture. Reassurance: small yellow papules on a red base, mostly over the trunk, in a well 2-day-old are erythema toxicum, a clinical diagnosis that clears without treatment; a smear, if done, shows eosinophils. Each decoy fits another rash.

How NBME framed it: question 2

5-year-old girl with 5 days of worsening dysuria and vaginal redness Her mother saw a little yellow discharge in her underwear No fever, vomiting or diarrhea; healthy, on no medications No history of sexual abuse vital signs normal moderate erythema over the vagina and whole perineum, perianal skin included no vesicles or pustules; scant white discharge at the introitus Rest of the exam normal; culture of the discharge pending

Most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

Competing answers
  • Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin: a genital rash with discharge raises a sexually transmitted infection; but gonorrhea and chlamydia give mucopurulent discharge, not white, and in a prepubertal child past the newborn period either would also prompt a sexual abuse evaluation.
  • Oral acyclovir: genital pain and redness; but herpes simplex virus gives painful vesicles on a red base, and there are none.
  • Oral amoxicillin: burning with urination suggests cystitis; but redness over the vulva and perineum with white discharge points to yeast.
  • Oral metronidazole: a vaginal discharge; but its spectrum is obligate anaerobic bacteria and protozoa such as Trichomonas vaginalis (it is the antibiotic of choice for bacterial vaginosis), and this is yeast; topical agents are preferred for superficial candidiasis.

Down to two: topical nystatin or oral amoxicillin. Topical nystatin: candidal vulvovaginitis in a girl past the diaper years. The stem opens on burning with urination and closes on a pending culture, while the diagnosis sits in the white discharge and the perineal-to-perianal redness. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, recent antibiotics and corticosteroids; none is required.

Management
By rash Erythema toxicum – reassurance: educate the parents about its benign course; it fades over 5 to 7 days and may recur for several weeks; no treatment is needed · Transient neonatal pustular melanosis – observe; no treatment is necessary · Milia – observe; reassurance about the benign, self-limited course; do not extract · Miliaria rubra – a cool environment, no overbundling, loose, thin, breathable cotton; a mild- to mid-potency topical steroid may be applied if severe · Cephalic pustulosis – observe (weeks to months); a topical antifungal such as ketoconazole can be used safely and may help; a low-potency steroid and avoiding oily emollients ⚠︎ · Seborrheic dermatitis – reassurance and watchful waiting; an emollient and gentle brushing with a soft brush can loosen the scale; topical ketoconazole is safe in infants · Irritant diaper dermatitis – a barrier such as zinc oxide or petrolatum, and frequent diaper changes; a short course of a low-potency steroid can be used if not improving within 2 to 3 days, or in moderate to severe cases · Candidal diaper dermatitis – topical nystatin with every diaper change, applied under the barrier ointment; switch to an azole (clotrimazole, miconazole or ketoconazole, twice daily for 7 to 10 days) if no improvement by 1 to 3 days; add oral nystatin for thrush; avoid a high-potency steroid under a diaper, which occludes
Not benign: red flags and the dangerous mimics Red flags: palms or soles involved in an otherwise erythema toxicum picture, vesicles or crusting, or fever or irritability; any one means the rash is not benign. Pustular melanosis, present at birth and nonerythematous, is the benign rash that may reach the palms and soles. Neonatal HSV: clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, days 5 to 14; PCR and IV acyclovir. Congenital syphilis: maculopapular rash that includes the palms and soles, snuffles, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, no pustules; IV penicillin. Staphylococcal pustulosis: localized pustules, vesicles or bullae that rupture to honey-colored crusts, in the diaper area or at a wound such as a circumcision; topical mupirocin. Blueberry muffin rash: TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus). Langerhans cell histiocytosis: looks seborrheic but is petechial and does not resolve. Maternal cold sores: do not diagnose HSV in a well 2-day-old with erythematous pustules and spared palms and soles; base the diagnosis on the morphology and the infant's well appearance.
Worse after it got better The diagnosis rests on the trajectory, not the morphology. A barrier is the correct and sufficient treatment for irritant dermatitis, so a rash that improved on it and then worsened has a superinfection, not a new diagnosis; a rash failing first-line therapy from the start would instead question the original diagnosis. Two examination findings name the cause: the rash involves the skinfolds, and it has satellite lesions, discrete red papules beyond the border of the main plaque, the most characteristic and near-specific feature of Candida. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases because the convex surfaces touch the wet diaper and the depths of the folds are protected; Candida thrives in the warm, occluded crease. Recent diarrhea is the risk factor, not a diagnosis: a higher local pH can increase fecal enzyme activity and damage the barrier, and Candida albicans from the gut then colonizes the skin. Expect it after recent diarrhea, recent antibiotics, or with oral thrush. The antifungal goes under the barrier, not instead of it, because the skin is still broken and still in contact with stool.
Reading the stem Run the spine: did first-line therapy work and then stop? Folds involved? Satellites? Does the rash leave the diaper area (scabies)? Is the diarrhea chronic, with perioral rash and alopecia (zinc)? Is any lesion itself a sexually transmitted infection? If none is, nothing licenses an abuse workup. Afebrile, eating and sleeping normally means not systemically ill; fussiness only during changes is local pain. Social details such as separated parents or day care raise abuse and contagion, but neither is an examination finding, and no affected classmate excludes contagion. The initial improvement on the barrier is the single most informative detail.
Other newborn skin findings Congenital dermal melanocytosis: blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, benign and self-resolving by age 3 to 5 years; document them on exam to avoid confusion with non-accidental trauma. Acrocyanosis (symmetric blue-purple hands and feet with crying or cold), cutis marmorata (symmetric lacy violaceous mottling of the limbs that changes with temperature) and harlequin color change (sharply demarcated redness of one side of the body) are clinical diagnoses that need no treatment.
Common wrong answers Oral amoxicillin for a refractory diaper rash: bacterial superinfection is real, but perianal streptococcal disease is bright red and sharply demarcated around the anus. Topical permethrin: scabies causes refractory diaper rash in infants, but it is diffuse across the trunk, axillae, palms and soles, with an affected contact. Oral zinc after a diarrheal illness: acrodermatitis enteropathica needs chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis and alopecia. Screening for sexual abuse: triggered by findings that are themselves sexually transmitted infections; a social detail is not a finding.
Pairs with Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the non-cutaneous half of the same principle (transplacental hormone, physiologic, self-limited) and vaginal discharge in a newborn girl: is the discharge white with perineal redness, or mucoid in a well newborn?
Transferable rule

Before choosing pure reassurance, scan the history for a modifiable exposure (bundling, a soap, a detergent, a medication, a position); when the history describes the environment, removing that exposure is the treatment. When a correct treatment works and then stops working, the diagnosis was not wrong; something was added. Ask what the first treatment does not cover, and look for the finding that identifies it.
